one_line: Better Stack beginner walkthrough of Docker logging: docker logs flags (tail, since, until, grep), the default json-file driver, how the official nginx image symlinks logs to stdout/stderr, daemon.json log options, and four logging strategies.
summary: The video demonstrates Docker logging with an nginx container on Windows/WSL. It shows how `docker logs` returns stdout/stderr, how to filter output with --tail, --since, --until and grep, and explains that the official nginx image symlinks access.log and error.log to /dev/stdout and /dev/stderr so Docker can capture them. It covers the log driver model (json-file default, local, none, syslog, journald, fluentd, cloud drivers) and shows configuring json-file rotation (max-size 20m, max-file 5, compress) and custom attributes via daemon.json log-opts. It closes with four strategies: host log driver, dedicated logging container, in-container shipper, and sidecar. The content is beginner-level and mostly a demo of standard Docker features, with no benchmarks or sponsorship.

key_ideas.idea: docker logs returns whatever a container writes to stdout and stderr, so the app's own logs are visible without extra setup.
key_ideas.detail: Access requests from nginx show up as HTTP GET lines each time the page is refreshed.

key_ideas.idea: The official nginx image makes its logs visible to Docker by symlinking access.log and error.log to /dev/stdout and /dev/stderr.
key_ideas.detail: Without those ln commands in the Dockerfile, the logging driver would not see nginx's log files at all. Custom images need the same trick.

key_ideas.idea: Filtering flags on docker logs keep output manageable on busy services.
key_ideas.detail: --tail N returns the last N lines, --since takes a relative duration, --until takes a cutoff, and piping to grep searches the output.

key_ideas.idea: The default json-file driver writes one JSON object per line on the host, and it does not rotate logs unless told to.
key_ideas.detail: Each entry has log, stream and time keys. Files live under the Docker data directory, named by container ID.

key_ideas.idea: Log rotation and compression are configured per daemon in daemon.json under log-driver and log-opts.
key_ideas.detail: The video sets max-size 20m, max-file 5 and compress true. Changes need a Docker daemon restart, and existing containers do not pick them up.

key_ideas.idea: Extra fields can be added to every log entry through log-opts env, which puts a container's environment variables under an attributes key.
key_ideas.detail: The video sets OS=Ubuntu and shows it in the JSON output, which helps with search and filtering.

key_ideas.idea: Remote log shipping is usually better done by a dedicated shipper such as Fluentd reading the local files, not by sending logs synchronously over the network from the daemon.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says network-sending drivers can add latency to containers.

key_ideas.idea: Four logging strategies: host log driver, dedicated logging container, in-container shipper, and sidecar. Each trades off differently.
key_ideas.detail: In-container shippers break the one-process-per-container rule and can add latency. Sidecars give per-app control but cost resources and complexity, so they suit large orgs.

techniques.name: Read container logs with filters
techniques.how: Run `docker ps` to get the container ID, then `docker logs <id>`. Add `--tail 5` for the last 5 lines, `--since 5m` or `--since 5h` for a time window, `--until 3m` for an upper bound, and combine them. Pipe through `grep GET` to search.
techniques.when: Debugging a running container or inspecting recent requests without dumping the full log.

techniques.name: Make a container's file logs visible to Docker
techniques.how: In the Dockerfile, run `ln -sf /dev/stdout /var/log/nginx/access.log` and `ln -sf /dev/stderr /var/log/nginx/error.log`, as the official nginx image does. Then anything the app writes to those files reaches `docker logs`.
techniques.when: Packaging a service that writes logs to files inside the container, so the Docker logging pipeline can collect them.

techniques.name: Rotate and compress json-file logs globally
techniques.how: Edit daemon.json (on Linux /etc/docker/daemon.json; on Windows/macOS ~/.docker/daemon.json, or via Docker Desktop settings). Set "log-driver": "json-file" and "log-opts": {"max-size": "20m", "max-file": "5", "compress": "true"}. Restart Docker, then recreate the containers.
techniques.when: Any host where the default json-file driver would otherwise grow without bound. Usually the default choice.

techniques.name: Stamp each log entry with custom fields
techniques.how: In daemon.json, add an "env" key inside log-opts with comma-separated variable names, for example "env": "OS". Set the variable with `docker run -e OS=Ubuntu`. The value appears under attributes in each JSON log line.
techniques.when: You need service or environment metadata on every log line for later search or filtering.

techniques.name: Choose a log architecture
techniques.how: Small or medium apps: keep the host json-file driver. Remote shipping: run a log shipper such as Fluentd that reads the json-file output. Several containers: a dedicated logging container that aggregates them. Per-app control in a large org: a sidecar container per app. Avoid putting shippers in the app container, because that adds a second process and can block the app.
techniques.when: Deciding how logs leave Docker hosts, based on scale and how much tailoring each service needs.

numbers.claim: Log rotation config in the demo: max-size 20 megabytes, max-file 5, compress true.
docker logs --tail 5 returns the last 5 entries.
Default json-file driver does not rotate logs unless configured.

hot_takes: Remote log drivers that ship directly to CloudWatch or GCP add latency, so a dedicated shipper is better practice. (The speaker states this as general guidance, with no measurement.)
Sidecar logging is probably overkill for small or medium apps and suits large orgs with independently tailored logging needs.

relevance.why: AgentOS runs infra with Prometheus/Grafana and OTel on Docker. The log-driver rotation and shipper-vs-sidecar tradeoffs are background for log handling in the L4 observability stack.
relevance.action: Check whether the AgentOS docker-compose services set log-driver and log-opts (max-size, max-file) so the proxy and vLLM containers do not fill the disk on the RTX 5090 box.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps long-running Claude Code runs, which can produce large logs. Log rotation and the sidecar-vs-in-container tradeoff apply when checkpointing long runs in containers.
relevance.action: If ProsHarness runs agents in Docker, set max-size and max-file in daemon.json so long checkpointed runs do not grow logs without bound.
